Compute similarity between spatial transcriptomics samples based on which
labels (e.g. cell types) border one another.

## Installation

```bash
pip install "git+https://github.com/edavidk7/friendlyspots@metrics-and-benchmarks#subdirectory=python"
```

Requires `pandas`, `numpy` and `scipy`. Also available as an
[R package](https://github.com/george-hall-ucl/friendlyspots/tree/main/R).

## Usage

`friendlyspots` is only compatible with original (non-HD) Visium.

```python
from friendlyspots import spatial_similarity

# Create one DataFrame per sample, with columns for array_row, array_col,
# label.
#   e.g. starting from a sample's AnnData object `adata`:
#   df1 = adata.obs[["array_row", "array_col"]].assign(
#       label=adata.obs["cell_type"]
#   )
samples = {"sample_1": df1, "sample_2": df2, "sample_3": df3}

sim = spatial_similarity(samples)
```

Returns a sample × sample DataFrame of similarity scores from 0 to 1, where 1
means spatially identical. With the default metric, 0 is the least similar pair
among the samples compared; other metrics give scores that don't depend on
which other samples are compared (see `metric` below).

Which metric to use: `"random_walk"` discounts how common each label is and
has no parameters, and `"moran"` compares each sample with random placement of
its own labels, separating composition from arrangement, with scores that
don't depend on sample size. To detect a rare cell type changing where it is,
use `"random_walk"` with `unit_diagonal=True`, which did best at that in the
[benchmarks](#benchmarks), though it also makes noise in rare labels count for
more. The default, `"euclidean"`, is kept for compatibility with earlier
results, but mostly reflects how much of each label samples have rather than
how labels are arranged.

### Options

- `normalize=False`: compare raw connection counts instead of proportions. This
  will make samples with different numbers of spots be considered spatially
  different even if their underlying spatial features are similar.
- `pools={"group_1": ["sample_1", "sample_2"], "group_2": ["sample_3"]}`: sum
  connection counts within groups before comparing.
- `unit_diagonal=True`: scale each sample's connection counts to
  $C_{ij} / \sqrt{C_{ii} C_{jj}}$, so every label's connections with itself are
  1, removing how much of each label there is. Rare labels then count for more,
  and so does noise in them. For `"euclidean"` and `"random_walk"`.
- `metric`: how connection counts are compared. All metrics other than the
  default give absolute scores, which don't depend on which other samples are
  compared, and require `normalize=True`.
  - `"euclidean"` (default): Euclidean distance between connection
    proportions, rescaled so the least similar pair scores 0.
  - `"random_walk"`: compares which labels each label borders, relative to its
    own total, so differences in how common each label is matter less. Simple,
    with no parameters. A label missing from one sample counts as a
    difference, in proportion to how common it is in the other.
  - `"moran"`: compares how far each pair of labels' joins (touching spots)
    are from what random placement of the sample's own labels on its own spots
    would give, as Moran's join-count z-scores, by the angle between samples'
    z-score vectors. Conditions on composition and on the spots' layout, and
    doesn't depend on sample size. Unrelated samples score about 0.5, opposite
    ones 0.
- `exact_tail=True`: for `"moran"`, score label pairs with fewer than 5
  expected joins by their exact tail probability rather than a normal
  approximation, so a chance join between two spots of a rare label doesn't
  count as a large deviation.

### How the metrics work

All metrics start from each sample's **connection counts**. Every spot has up
to 6 neighbors on the Visium grid. For labels $i$ and $j$,

$$C_{ij} = \left|\lbrace (u, v) : u, v \text{ neighbors}, \ \text{label}(u) = i, \ \text{label}(v) = j \rbrace\right|,$$

so each touching pair of spots is counted once from each side and $C$ is
symmetric. The default `"euclidean"` metric divides $C$ by its total, so it
sums to 1, and takes the Euclidean distance between samples, divided by the
largest such distance among the samples compared.

These proportions mix two things: how much of each label a sample has
(**composition**) and how the labels are arranged. A sample with twice as many
spots of one label has more contacts involving that label even if the layout
is the same. The two other metrics separate these in different ways.

#### `"random_walk"`

Take a random spot of label $i$ and step to a random one of its neighbors. The
probability that the neighbor has label $j$ is

$$P_i(j) = \frac{\tilde C_{ij}}{r_i}, \qquad \tilde C = C + I, \qquad r_i = \sum_j \tilde C_{ij}.$$

In matrix form, $P = D^{-1} \tilde C$ with $D = \mathrm{diag}(r)$: the
transition matrix of a Markov chain on labels. Each row $P_i$ is a probability
distribution describing what label $i$ borders. Having more spots of label $i$
scales the whole row $C_{i\cdot}$, so $P_i$ doesn't change: the abundance of
label $i$ itself drops out.

The identity matrix $I$ adds one self loop per label. With thousands of
connections per sample it barely changes labels that are present, but it makes
every row a distribution: a label absent from a sample becomes a state the
walk never leaves, $P_i(i) = 1$, so it can be compared with the same label in
a sample that has it.

Two samples $a$ and $b$ are compared label by label, using the square root of
the Jensen-Shannon divergence with base-2 logarithms, which lies in $[0, 1]$:

$$D_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{KL}\left(P_i^a  \parallel  M_i\right) + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{KL}\left(P_i^b  \parallel  M_i\right)}, \qquad M_i = \tfrac{1}{2} \left(P_i^a + P_i^b\right).$$

Labels that are more common should count for more, so the label distances are
averaged with weights $\omega_i$, the label's share of connections averaged
over the two samples:

$$d(a, b) = \sum_i \omega_i D_i, \qquad \omega_i = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{r_i^a}{\sum_k r_k^a} + \frac{r_i^b}{\sum_k r_k^b}\right).$$

The weights sum to 1, and a label absent from one sample gets about half its
share in the other, so missing labels count in proportion to how common they
are where they appear. $\pi_i = r_i / \sum_k r_k$ is also a stationary
distribution of the chain ($\pi P = \pi$, as $\tilde C$ is symmetric): if
every label can reach every other, it's the long-run share of time the walk
spends on label $i$. The similarity is $1 - d(a, b)$.

#### `unit_diagonal`

This changes each sample's connection counts before `"euclidean"` or
`"random_walk"` compares them. With one self loop per label, $\tilde C = C + I$,
as for `"random_walk"`, `unit_diagonal=True` uses

$$U_{ij} = \frac{\tilde C_{ij}}{\sqrt{\tilde C_{ii} \, \tilde C_{jj}}},$$

like turning a covariance matrix into a correlation matrix: $U_{ii} = 1$ for
every label, so $U$ no longer reflects how many spots each label has, only how
labels' connections compare with their own connections with themselves. A
label with few spots has a small $\tilde C_{ii}$, so its connections are
scaled up, along with any noise in them.

#### `"moran"`

For labels $a \le b$, the join count $J_{ab}$ is the number of edges joining a
spot of label $a$ to one of label $b$: $J_{ab} = C_{ab}$ for $a \ne b$, and
$J_{aa} = C_{aa} / 2$, as $C$ counts each edge from both ends. Moran's (1948)
non-free null places the sample's own labels on its own spots uniformly at
random, keeping the number of spots $n_a$ of each label. With $n$ spots, $m$
edges, $d_p$ the number of neighbors of spot $p$, $k_2 = \sum_p d_p (d_p - 1)$
the ordered pairs of distinct edges sharing a spot, and the falling factorial
$x^{(r)} = x (x - 1) \cdots (x - r + 1)$, the mean and second moment of a join
count are (Cliff & Ord 1981)

$$E[J_{aa}] = m \frac{n_a^{(2)}}{n^{(2)}}, \qquad E[J_{aa}^2] = E[J_{aa}] + k_2 \frac{n_a^{(3)}}{n^{(3)}} + \left(m (m - 1) - k_2\right) \frac{n_a^{(4)}}{n^{(4)}},$$

$$E[J_{ab}] = 2 m \frac{n_a n_b}{n^{(2)}}, \qquad E[J_{ab}^2] = E[J_{ab}] + k_2 \frac{n_a n_b (n_a + n_b - 2)}{n^{(3)}} + 4 \left(m (m - 1) - k_2\right) \frac{n_a^{(2)} n_b^{(2)}}{n^{(4)}}.$$

$E[J^2]$ sums over ordered pairs of edges: an edge with itself ($m$ pairs, 2
spots), two edges sharing a spot ($k_2$ pairs, 3 spots) and two disjoint edges
(4 spots), each with the probability that those spots get the required labels.
With $\mathrm{Var}(J) = E[J^2] - E[J]^2$, each label pair gets the z-score

$$z_{ab} = \frac{J_{ab} - E[J_{ab}]}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(J_{ab})}},$$

positive when $a$ and $b$ touch more than random placement predicts and
negative when less, whatever the composition. Samples $u$ and $v$ are compared
by the angle between their vectors $\mathbf{z}$ of all pairs $a \le b$:

$$\mathrm{sim}(u, v) = 1 - \frac{1}{\pi} \arccos \frac{\mathbf{z}_u \cdot \mathbf{z}_v}{\lVert \mathbf{z}_u \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{z}_v \rVert}.$$

The same arrangement on a larger sample gives z-scores larger by about
$\sqrt{m}$, which the angle ignores, and no other samples are involved. With
`pools`, observed joins, means and variances are each summed over a pool's
samples before standardizing.

When a pair expects few joins, $J$ is close to Poisson, and the normal z-score
overstates deviations: two touching spots of a label with 2 spots in a section
of $n = 3000$ expect $E \approx 6 / n$ joins, giving $z \approx 22$, as much as
a large real pattern. With `exact_tail=True`, pairs with $E < 5$ instead get
$z = \Phi^{-1}\left(P(J' < J) + \tfrac{1}{2} P(J' = J)\right)$ for $J' \sim
\mathrm{Poisson}(E)$, about 3.1 in this example.

### Benchmarks

How well each metric retrieves samples known to belong together, as mean
average precision (mAP: 1 means every sample ranks all samples of its group
above all others). Composition only is a baseline, not a metric option: it
compares label proportions, ignoring where spots are. Best per row in bold.
Scripts and data downloads to reproduce these are in
[`benchmarks/`](https://github.com/edavidk7/friendlyspots/tree/metrics-and-benchmarks/python/benchmarks).

| Dataset | Task | Chance | Composition only | `euclidean` | `random_walk` | `rw`, `unit_diagonal` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Synthetic | Arrangement, fixed composition | 0.2 | 0.25 | **0.89** | 0.85 | 0.84 |
| Synthetic | Arrangement, varied composition | 0.2 | 0.22 | 0.37 | **0.72** | **0.72** |
| Synthetic | ... + boundary label noise (30%) | 0.2 | 0.23 | 0.37 | **0.71** | **0.71** |
| Synthetic | ... + random label noise (15%) | 0.2 | 0.23 | 0.37 | 0.44 | **0.47** |
| Pig esophagus | Time point | 0.40 | 0.61 | 0.59 | 0.59 | **0.63** |
| Human cortex | Donor | 0.42 | 0.96 | 0.93 | **1.00** | **1.00** |
| Human cortex | Adjacent section | 0.28 | 0.85 | **0.86** | **0.86** | **0.86** |
| Human cortex | Donor, random label noise (15%) | 0.42 | 0.95 | 0.94 | **0.97** | 0.92 |
| Human cortex | Adjacent section, random label noise (15%) | 0.28 | 0.82 | 0.84 | **0.89** | 0.72 |
| Human cortex | Donor, random label noise (30%) | 0.42 | 0.96 | 0.93 | **0.97** | 0.89 |
| Human cortex | Adjacent section, random label noise (30%) | 0.28 | **0.85** | 0.84 | **0.85** | 0.70 |
| Human cortex | Donor, random crops | 0.37 | 0.61 | 0.60 | **0.72** | 0.68 |
| Human cortex | Section, random crops | 0.13 | 0.29 | 0.30 | **0.38** | 0.33 |
| Human heart | Patient group | 0.46 | 0.79 | 0.76 | **0.81** | 0.53 |

Synthetic scores are means over 10 random datasets (standard deviations
0.03-0.08); noise and crop scores are means over 5 random draws.

#### Detecting small alterations

How well each setting tells a section with a small alteration apart from the
same section with only label noise, as AUC: the probability that an altered
pair of sections is further apart than a pair differing only by noise, so 0.5
means no better than chance and 1 always. Noise is applied independently to
both sections of a pair. Alterations are compact patches of 10 / 20 spots
(about 1% of a section):

- **Niche cluster**: a rare cell type, otherwise scattered over 2% of the
  spots, gathers into a cluster at the interface between the two most common
  labels. Its number of spots is unchanged, so only its arrangement differs.
- **New domain**: an island of an existing label appears inside a region of a
  label it otherwise doesn't touch.

Noise is random label flips (5% or 10% of spots), or boundary jitter (30% of
spots bordering another label take a neighbor's label). `"rw"` is
`"random_walk"`. Best per row and size in bold.

| Dataset | Alteration | Noise | Composition only | `euclidean` | `random_walk` | `rw`, `unit_diagonal` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Synthetic | Niche cluster | random flips 5% | 0.50 / 0.49 | 0.55 / 0.68 | 0.62 / 0.74 | **0.95** / **1.00** |
| Synthetic | New domain | random flips 5% | **0.61** / **0.78** | 0.57 / 0.71 | 0.55 / 0.56 | 0.50 / 0.51 |
| Synthetic | Niche cluster | random flips 10% | 0.54 / 0.53 | 0.60 / 0.64 | 0.57 / 0.67 | **0.86** / **0.99** |
| Synthetic | New domain | random flips 10% | 0.60 / 0.66 | **0.62** / **0.68** | 0.52 / 0.51 | 0.47 / 0.51 |
| Synthetic | Niche cluster | boundary jitter 30% | 0.48 / 0.48 | 0.55 / 0.73 | 0.66 / 0.88 | **0.84** / **1.00** |
| Synthetic | New domain | boundary jitter 30% | 0.59 / 0.74 | 0.66 / 0.83 | **0.93** / **0.94** | 0.61 / 0.69 |
| Pig esophagus | Niche cluster | random flips 5% | 0.57 / 0.57 | 0.60 / 0.68 | 0.61 / 0.78 | **0.71** / **0.85** |
| Pig esophagus | New domain | random flips 5% | **0.61** / 0.65 | 0.53 / **0.70** | 0.48 / 0.49 | 0.48 / 0.52 |
| Pig esophagus | Niche cluster | random flips 10% | 0.47 / 0.42 | 0.46 / 0.57 | 0.52 / 0.61 | **0.65** / **0.86** |
| Pig esophagus | New domain | random flips 10% | 0.51 / 0.57 | **0.56** / **0.69** | 0.49 / 0.50 | 0.55 / 0.51 |
| Pig esophagus | Niche cluster | boundary jitter 30% | 0.51 / 0.43 | **0.63** / 0.77 | 0.59 / 0.88 | 0.60 / **0.96** |
| Pig esophagus | New domain | boundary jitter 30% | 0.50 / 0.62 | **0.66** / **0.83** | 0.60 / 0.64 | 0.43 / 0.36 |
| Human cortex | Niche cluster | random flips 5% | 0.52 / 0.53 | 0.55 / 0.75 | 0.56 / 0.69 | **0.95** / **1.00** |

| Human heart | New domain | boundary jitter 30% | **0.75** / **0.84** | 0.58 / 0.64 | 0.63 / 0.69 | 0.53 / 0.53 |

`unit_diagonal=True` makes `"random_walk"` far more sensitive to a rare cell
type changing niche, but less to a new domain of a common label, which plain
`"random_walk"` detects well when noise is at boundaries.

- **Synthetic**: generated tissue sections of random size, shape and
  orientation with 4 labels, in 6 arrangements (5 sections each): two layer
  orders, rings, smooth patches, randomly assigned patches and fully mixed.
  Composition is either the same for all sections or varies between them, so
  arrangement can be tested separately from composition.
- **Pig esophagus**: the 10 sections of the package's test data (Durkin et
  al. 2026), labelled by cell type: pre-implant, 1, 3 and 6 months after
  implantation, and native tissue. The task is to retrieve sections of the
  same time point.
- **Human cortex**: 12 sections of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Maynard et
  al. 2021) with manual annotations of cortical layers, from 3 donors, cut as
  pairs of adjacent sections. Also tested with random label noise, and with
  random crops of ~40% of each section, whose composition depends on where
  they fall while the layer order stays the same.
- **Human heart**: 15 sections after myocardial infarction and from controls
  (Kuppe et al. 2022), labelled by each spot's dominant cell type. The task is
  to retrieve sections of the same patient group: myogenic (control and
  remote zone), ischaemic or fibrotic.

### Example

Uses four mouse brain sections from 10x Genomics (two anterior, two posterior),
with each spot labelled by its most enriched of five marker genes.

<details><summary>Setup: download and label the data, define plotting helpers (click to expand)</summary>

```{python setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, results = "hide"}
# To rebuild this README from README.Rmd, run knitr::knit("README.Rmd") in R
# from the python/ directory, with RETICULATE_PYTHON set to a Python that has
# friendlyspots installed (rmarkdown::render breaks the <details> block).
# Requires squidpy, matplotlib and seaborn.
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import squidpy as sq

markers = ["Mbp", "Slc17a7", "Penk", "Hpca", "Gabra6"]
ids = {
    "anterior_1": "V1_Mouse_Brain_Sagittal_Anterior",
    "anterior_2": "V1_Mouse_Brain_Sagittal_Anterior_Section_2",
    "posterior_1": "V1_Mouse_Brain_Sagittal_Posterior",
    "posterior_2": "V1_Mouse_Brain_Sagittal_Posterior_Section_2",
}
cache = Path.home() / ".cache" / "friendlyspots"

adatas = {}
labels = {}
for name, sample_id in ids.items():
    adata = sq.datasets.visium(sample_id, base_dir=cache)
    adata.var_names_make_unique()
    counts = adata[:, markers].X.toarray()
    top = (counts / counts.mean(axis=0)).argmax(axis=1)
    adatas[name] = adata
    labels[name] = np.array(markers)[top]


palette = ["#CC79A7", "#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#F0E442", "#009E73"]
colors = dict(zip(sorted(markers), palette))


def plot_slices(samples):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(samples), layout="constrained")
    for ax, (name, df) in zip(axes, samples.items()):
        ax.scatter(
            df["array_col"],
            -df["array_row"] * np.sqrt(3),
            c=df["label"].map(colors),
            s=3,
            linewidths=0,
        )
        ax.set_title(name)
        ax.set_aspect("equal")
        ax.axis("off")
    handles = [
        plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", linestyle="", color=color, label=label)
        for label, color in colors.items()
    ]
    fig.legend(
        handles=handles,
        loc="outside lower center",
        ncol=len(colors),
        frameon=False,
    )
    plt.show()


def plot_similarity(sim):
    style = {"font.size": 14, "font.weight": "bold", "figure.autolayout": True}
    with plt.rc_context(style):
        ax = sns.heatmap(
            sim,
            mask=np.tril(np.ones(sim.shape, dtype=bool), k=-1),
            annot=True,
            fmt=".2f",
            cmap="inferno",
            vmin=0,
            vmax=1,
            square=True,
            cbar_kws={"label": "Similarity"},
        )
        ax.invert_yaxis()
        plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right")
    plt.show()
```

</details>

Each sample is a DataFrame of spot array coordinates and labels:

```{python samples}
from friendlyspots import spatial_similarity

samples = {
    name: adata.obs[["array_row", "array_col"]].assign(label=labels[name])
    for name, adata in adatas.items()
}
print(samples["anterior_1"].head())
```

```{python slices, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3.5, dpi = 300}
plot_slices(samples)
```

```{python similarity, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5, out.width = "50%"}
sim = spatial_similarity(samples)
print(sim.round(2))
plot_similarity(sim)
```

## Citation

The algorithm and original implementation of `friendlyspots` are based on the
methodology in:

- Durkin _et al_. "Functional integration of an autologous engineered esophagus
  in a large-animal model." _Nature Biotechnology_ (2026).
- Budinger _et al_. "An in vivo and in vitro spatiotemporal profile of human
  midbrain development." _Nature Communications_ (2026).
